title: First declension: ἀρχή, ἡμέρα, δόξα, μαθητής

objectives.can: Parse and form first-declension nouns, feminine and masculine.

explanation.summary: The first declension holds most feminine nouns and a smaller group of masculines. It has three feminine patterns in the singular (η, pure α, mixed α) and one masculine pattern, but the plural is the same for all.

sections.heading: Three feminine patterns in the singular
body: The first declension is the declension of the long vowel -α- or -η- in the stem. Its feminine nouns differ only in the singular, and only in the vowel before the endings.

The first pattern has η throughout: ἀρχή, ἀρχῆς, ἀρχῇ, ἀρχήν. The second has α throughout, and is the pattern of nouns whose stem ends in ε, ι or ρ, such as ἡμέρα and καρδία. The third, the 'mixed' pattern, has α in the nominative and accusative but η in the genitive and dative, as in δόξα, δόξης, δόξῃ, δόξαν. Words like θάλασσα and γλῶσσα follow the same pattern. The tables below show φωνή (η pattern) and γλῶσσα (mixed pattern) rather than ἀρχή and δόξα, because those two are fuller in the texts: the tables are built from attested forms, and ἀρχή and δόξα lack some of them.

So a learner meeting a nominative in -α cannot yet tell whether it is pure or mixed; the genitive shows it. A dictionary gives the genitive for that reason. In the text, the forms in the tables below tell you which pattern a noun follows.

sections.heading: The plural is the same for all
body: Whatever its singular pattern, a feminine noun of the first declension has the plural endings -αι, -ων, -αις, -ας. Compare the plural of the second declension, -οι, -ων, -οις, -ους: the genitive plural -ων is the same in every declension and every gender.

sections.heading: Masculine nouns in -ης and -ας
body: A number of masculine nouns belong to the first declension. Most end in -ης in the nominative (μαθητής, προφήτης), a few in -ας (νεανίας). They follow the feminine endings, with two differences: the genitive singular is -ου (like the second declension), and the nominative singular has -ς. The article shows the masculine gender: ὁ μαθητής, τοῦ μαθητοῦ. The vocative of these nouns differs and is taught later.
The plural is the same as that of feminine nouns: μαθηταί, μαθητῶν, μαθηταῖς, μαθητάς.

sections.heading: Reading the accent and the iota
body: The dative singular of the first declension has an iota subscript in all four patterns (ἀρχῇ, ἡμέρᾳ, δόξῃ, μαθητῇ). It is the clearest mark of the dative. The genitive plural is -ων, and in this declension the accent regularly falls on it as a circumflex (μαθητῶν, ψυχῶν).

misunderstandings: Not every feminine noun belongs to the first declension. Some feminine nouns have second-declension endings (ἡ ὁδός) and many are of the third (ἡ πόλις). Look at the endings and at the article.
A nominative in -α is not always the same pattern: ἡμέρα keeps α in the genitive (ἡμέρας), δόξα changes to η (δόξης).
Masculine nouns in -ης are not feminine. ὁ μαθητής takes the masculine article and masculine adjectives, even though its endings resemble the feminine's.
The accusative plural -ας is not the genitive singular -ας: the article and the sentence tell them apart (τὰς ἡμέρας, accusative plural; τῆς ἡμέρας, genitive singular).

deeper.heading: Why α sometimes becomes η
body: In Attic Greek, which is the model of the grammars, a stem in long α changed to η, except after ε, ι or ρ. In Hellenistic Greek, including the New Testament, the older patterns are still recognised, but some forms are found that do not follow them exactly, and a few nouns vary. Treat the three patterns as the norm and learn exceptions as you meet them.
